items.title: Unitary method
items.content: Find the value or quantity for one unit first. Direct proportion: multiply the one-unit value by the required units. Inverse proportion: total work/resource stays constant when assumptions hold.

items.title: Check relationship and units
items.content: Identify whether the problem is direct or inverse before calculating. Keep rates and time units consistent; state assumptions about equal units or productivity.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Use a small proportional table when several quantities change.
Check whether the answer should rise or fall before calculating.

items.title: Value of one unit
items.content: Worked example: 7 pens cost ₹84, so one pen costs ₹12.

items.title: Direct proportion
items.content: When one quantity increases with the other at a fixed rate, scale both by the same factor. Worked example: 7 pens cost ₹84; 12 cost \(12\times12=₹144\).

items.title: Inverse proportion
items.content: When more of one resource reduces the amount needed of another for fixed work, use a constant product. Worked example: 4 equal pumps empty a tank in 9 hours; 6 take \(4\cdot9/6=6\) hours.

items.title: Several units and compound rates
items.content: Work one stage at a time and keep units. Worked example: 3 machines make 180 parts in 2 hours; at equal rates, 5 machines in 4 hours make \(180(5/3)(4/2)=600\) parts.

items.title: Recognising proportionality
items.content: Direct: more items cost more at fixed unit price. Inverse: more equal workers take less time for fixed work. Neither applies if the rate changes. Worked example: 3 identical notebooks cost ₹45, so 5 cost ₹75 at the same unit price.

items.title: Cost or quantity by direct scaling
items.content: Find one unit, then multiply. Worked example: 9 m of cloth cost ₹1,350; 4 m cost \(1350/9\times4=₹600\).

items.title: Workers and time
items.content: Use workers × days constant only for equal work rates and fixed total work. Worked example: 5 equal workers take 12 days; 10 take 5 × 12/10 = 6 days for the same job.

items.title: Speed, time and distance
items.content: For fixed distance, speed and time are inverse; for fixed time, distance and speed are direct. Worked example: 60 km at 30 km/h takes 2 h; at 40 km/h it takes 1.5 h.

items.title: Multi-stage unitary problem
items.content: Find the one-unit rate then scale each independent quantity, checking dimensions at each step. Worked example: 4 printers make 240 pages in 3 min; 6 printers in 5 min make 240 × 6/4 × 5/3 = 600 pages at equal rates.

items.title: Derive direct proportion
items.content: If each unit contributes a fixed amount \(k\), total for \(n\) units is \(kn\); the ratio amount/units remains constant.

items.title: Derive inverse proportion for fixed work
items.content: If one worker completes \(r\) units of work per time, \(n\) equal workers complete at rate \(nr\). Fixed work \(W=nr t\), so \(nt\) is constant.

items.title: Dimensional check
items.content: Multiplying a per-item rate by items cancels item units and leaves currency; unit cancellation helps detect a wrong operation.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Using direct proportion for inverse situations
items.content: Ask what happens when one quantity doubles; fixed-work time should halve when equal workers double.

items.title: Skipping the one-unit step
items.content: Write the per-unit rate with units before scaling.

items.title: Ignoring changing conditions
items.content: Proportional methods require constant unit rate, speed, or productivity.

items.title: Mixing time units
items.content: Convert minutes and hours consistently before using a rate.

keyTakeaways: Unitary method begins with one unit.
Inverse proportion applies only when a product remains fixed.
Units reveal whether a rate calculation is sensible.

questionTypes: Cost or quantity by direct scaling
proofsAndDerivations: Derive inverse proportion for fixed work
